title: Majority Says ICE Enforcement Has Gone Too Far Before Midterms
excerpt: Fox News and Pew polling show 53% of voters — and two-thirds of Hispanic voters — say enforcement has gone too far, eroding Trump's 2024 gains weeks before the November 3 vote.
body:
• A Fox News poll conducted September 11-14 found 53% of registered voters say immigration enforcement has gone too far, including 60% of independents and two-thirds of Hispanic voters.
  • Pew Research Center found approval among Hispanic voters who backed Donald Trump in 2024 has fallen from 93% in early 2025 to 57% in its September 28-October 4 survey.
  • ICE reported two straight months above 50,000 arrests through September, while analysts cited by Al Jazeera say about 70% of people in ICE detention have no criminal record — a gap the administration disputes by counting pending charges.
  • For immigrant families, the practical stakes are set on November 3: the midterms decide control of both chambers of Congress, which fund ICE and oversee its tactics, so checking your registration and polling place now is the concrete step.

Immigration enforcement has become a central fault line in the November 3 midterm elections, with a majority of voters now saying the crackdown has gone too far, according to polling reported by Al Jazeera. Republicans are defending majorities in both chambers, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement tactics are drawing scrutiny beyond the border debate that dominated 2024.

What the polls show

The Fox News survey of 1,211 registered voters found 53% believe enforcement has gone too far, a view held by 87% of Democrats and 60% of independents. Among those who said it had gone too far, 49% said the wrong people are being targeted and 45% cited excessive force. Trump's approval on immigration stood at 43% in that poll, and the parties were nearly tied on which would handle immigration better, at 49% for Republicans and 48% for Democrats — erasing an advantage Republicans held for four years.

Pew Research Center recorded a parallel erosion among Hispanic voters. Trump won nearly 48% of the Latino vote in 2024, up 12 points from 2020, according to Pew exit polling cited by Al Jazeera. Among Hispanic Trump voters, approval has since fallen from 93% at the start of 2025 to 57%. Overall, Pew put Trump's job approval at 30%, with 41% expressing confidence in his immigration decisions, down from 53% in November 2024.

"Voters now think of immigration policy as ICE crackdowns, and many say these have been too aggressive."

— Daron Shaw, Republican pollster for the Fox News survey

The argument over who is being arrested

The administration says enforcement targets serious criminals. The Department of Homeland Security has said its operations focus on the most serious offenders, and it counts people with pending charges in its figure of roughly 70% of detainees with a criminal record or charges. White House border adviser Tom Homan said in July that the administration needs more arrests and more deportations.

Critics point to a different count. Al Jazeera reported that the Deportation Data Project, which analyses government datasets, puts the share of people currently in ICE detention with no criminal record at about 70%. The case highlighted in the report involved a 23-year-old in Houston arrested during a traffic stop in August who, her family says, was brought to the United States at about age five, was an honour-roll student and has no criminal record. She remains in custody. ICE said arrests exceeded 50,000 in each of two consecutive months through September, above the prior record of 43,900 in June.

Pushback inside both parties

The debate is not only partisan. Florida Republican Representative Maria Elvira Salazar ran a September advertisement telling the president directly that some enforcement efforts have gone too far, citing arrests of people without criminal records. Other Republicans argue that earlier administrations created the backlog now being cleared. Democrats, meanwhile, are campaigning on abolishing or sharply curtailing ICE; the Hidalgo County Democratic chair in Texas told Al Jazeera he hopes Democrats abolish the agency.

What it means for Indian and other immigrant families

For Indian-American and other immigrant households, the numbers matter because enforcement is no longer framed only around border crossings or serious convictions. When independent analysts say most detainees have no conviction, any encounter — a traffic stop, a workplace visit — carries higher risk. Families with pending applications should keep status documents accessible and, where eligible, confirm voter registration before November 3; Congress controls ICE funding and oversight.

What happens next

Voting on November 3 will test whether dissatisfaction with tactics outweighs support for stricter enforcement. Fox News polling shows immigration trails only cost of living and the economy as a voter priority, even though just 8% name it as their top issue. If Hispanic and independent voters who moved toward Republicans in 2024 stay home or switch, competitive House districts in Texas, Florida and the Southwest are the first places the shift would show.
